# Padakusalamāṇavajātaka (Ja 432)
**ID:** Ja 432
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Padakusalamāṇavajātaka* (Ja 432; also called *Padamānava Jātaka*) is an extensive narrative belonging to the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral; Rahula 1956]. Maurice Winternitz characterizes it as a longer fairy-tale composition in prose and verse containing inserted narratives [Winternitz 1933]. According to the frame narrative set at Jetavana, the Buddha recounts the tale concerning a seven-year-old householder's son in Sāvatthi who possessed an innate genius for recognizing and tracking human footsteps [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883].
The story of the past relates that the Bodhisatta was born from the union of a captured human brāhmaṇa and a horse-headed, man-eating yakkhinī (Assamukhī) living in a cave [Sutherland 1991; Rahula 1956; Luce et al. 1970]. After learning the secret of his origins, the Bodhisatta carries his enfeebled father across a river that delimits the yakkhinī's territory; upon reaching safety beyond her boundary, the distraught mother dies of a broken heart [DeCaroli 1999; Clark 1994]. Gifted with extraordinary tracking abilities—associated with a *cintāmaṇi* jewel—the Bodhisatta enters human society and is tested by a king who covertly steals his own treasury to challenge the youth's skills [Clark 1994; Tambiah 1976]. Exposing the ruler himself as the culprit, the Bodhisatta proclaims a verse warning the populace that "water is ablaze" and their protector has turned robber, leading the subjects to depose and slay the corrupt monarch [Moore 2016; Tambiah 1976]. The narrative also features an incompetent lay "devil-doctor" who mistakes an elderly woman in a cave for a yakṣī [DeCaroli 2004].
Scholars have identified significant non-Buddhist parallels to the tale; Serge d'Oldenburg noted close counterparts in the Jain *Samyaktvakaumudī* and in commentaries on the *Uttarajjhayaṇa* [Shyu 2008]. Computational analysis by DharmaNexus identifies text reuse between the Pali verses and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, as well as alignments with Kṣemendra's *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* in the Tibetan canon (D4155) [DharmaNexus]. Visually, episodes from the Jātaka, including the horse-faced Aśvamukhī and her Bodhisatta son, are famously illustrated in temple murals of early Pagan in Burma [Luce et al. 1970].
